name: Hexagon
//: Hexagon recognizes a closed token language (spec/lexer.md §1), so this grammar
mirrors that inventory rather than guessing. Identifier classes follow §3.1:
start class is syntax, so an uppercase-start name is a type/constructor role and a
non-uppercase-start name is a term/binder role, decided by the literal first
codepoint alone. Hard keywords are §4.1; contextual keywords (§4.2) lex as ordinary
names and are only matched here in the positions the spec lists. Constructs the
§10 requires a diagnostic for are painted invalid.illegal so the editor shows
the same errors the compiler would. (Not "the lexer rejects": some rows, the
`true`/`false` redirect among them, lex fine and are the parser's to refuse.)

patterns.//: Before #operators: spec/lexer.md §8.2 requires `||` to be one forbidden run pointing at `or`, never two pattern bars.

spec/doc-comments.md §2.1: a block comment is a doc comment when `(**` is followed by a character that is neither `)` nor `*`. §2.2's two carve-outs are exactly the lookahead's two characters: `(**)` stays an ordinary empty block comment, and `(***`, `(****…` stay ordinary so rulers and banners never become documentation. A line-ending `(**` is a doc opener too — the character after it is the newline — which is §3.1's newline-first body idiom; vscode-textmate appends that newline to every line before matching, so the lookahead sees it. Written negatively rather than as `(?=[^)*])` because language-configuration.json's `onEnterRules` need the same predicate against lines that carry no newline, and one spelling for one rule is worth more than the one case the two forms differ on: a `(**` with nothing after it at all, which hexc reads as ordinary (`#scanBlockComment` requires a character) and this rule would read as documentation. Unreachable here — the appended newline is always that character — and both scopes are one colour anyway.
patterns.name: comment.block.documentation.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/comments.md §3: block comments nest.
patterns.name: comment.block.hexagon

patterns.//: begin/end rather than match, so a bidirectional control inside the comment body still gets its own scope (§3.2 prohibits them in comments too). There is no line doc form to match ahead of this one: spec/doc-comments.md §2.3 revoked the `///` reservation unspent, so `///` is this rule with a `/` as its first character of text — the grammar does not count slashes.
patterns.name: comment.line.double-slash.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/comments.md §3: `*)` at depth zero is a hard error, not `*` then `)`.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unmatched-comment-close.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/comments.md §3.1: `/*` is JavaScript's opener and is detected, never lexed as `/` then `*`. The region it opens is painted as one error, mirroring the compiler's scan-to-`*/` recovery — a pasted JSDoc block is one region, not a line of error followed by `@param` painted as an invalid character. Ending at `$` instead would say that, and would also let #tab-indentation fire on a tab inside the comment body, which the compiler explicitly does not diagnose. The bail-out guard is what stops a half-typed `/*` from repainting the file; see the //line-bail-guard note.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.javascript-comment.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/comments.md §3.1: a stray `*/` where a token may begin, which Hexagon spells `*)`.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.javascript-comment.hexagon

strings.//: spec/lexer.md §6: one composite String token; may span physical newlines.
strings.name: string.quoted.double.hexagon

string-escape.//: spec/lexer.md §6.2 is the complete escape inventory; no legacy JS escapes.
string-escape.name: constant.character.escape.hexagon

//: spec/lexer.md §6.2: a `\u{...}` escape must name a Unicode scalar value —
at most U+10FFFF and never a surrogate. These run before #string-escape so a
well-formed-looking but out-of-range escape loses to the invalid rule.
Leading zeros are legal, hence the `0*`.

patterns.//: A surrogate: the whole D800-DFFF block, so the second nibble is 8 through F.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unicode-escape.hexagon

patterns.//: Above U+10FFFF.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unicode-escape.hexagon

patterns.//: More than six digits, whatever their value.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unicode-escape.hexagon

bidirectional-control.//: spec/lexer.md §3.2: literal bidirectional controls are prohibited throughout source, including comments and strings — this is the trojan-source class, so it is included in those contexts too, not only at the top level.
bidirectional-control.name: invalid.illegal.bidirectional-control.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §6.2: `\u{...}` must be 1-6 hex digits naming a scalar value.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.unicode-escape.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §6.2: bare `#{` is reserved for future Debug interpolation; write `\#{`.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.reserved-interpolation.hexagon

interpolation.//: spec/lexer.md §6.1: the hole is lexed recursively with the normal inventory.
interpolation.name: meta.embedded.line.hexagon

brace-group.//: Keeps a record literal's `}` inside a hole from closing the interpolation.

reserved-identifier.//: spec/lexer.md §3.2: leading `__` is reserved for compiler-generated names (#425).
reserved-identifier.name: invalid.illegal.reserved-identifier.hexagon

//: `extern from "specifier"` is the only extern form that opens an indented block,
and it is always top-level, so the block ends at the next line starting in
column zero. The FFI contextual keywords (spec/lexer.md §4.2) are recognized only
in here: `get`, `set`, `new`, `default` and friends are ordinary names elsewhere.
extern-from-block.name: meta.extern.hexagon

patterns.//: `enum Direction = ...` / `class Foo` — the described foreign type is uppercase-start.
`export method get(...)`, `export get status(...)`, `export static method of(...)`.

spec/effects.md §6.1's trusted purity claim. `pure` is a contextual modifier on a user-written extern `fun` and an ordinary name everywhere else, so the lookahead requires the `fun` — which also keeps it off the extern `let` and `type` rows, where FFI Part 4 §4.5 refuses the claim outright.
`export new(...)` constructor description, and the `default` import position.

//: Names the thing being declared. `fun` always introduces a function; `let`/`var`
introduce one only when a parameter list or type-parameter list follows
(stdlib/Seq.hex leans on this distinction heavily).
Each name alternative excludes the §4.1 hard keywords as well as uppercase
starts and the reserved leading `__` (#425). These rules are included ahead of
#keywords, so without
that guard they would claim the keyword first and paint `let true = 1` or
`let if = 1` — both §10 hard errors — as ordinary, valid binders (#154). The
guard's trailing boundary lookahead is what keeps `let iffy` and `let format`
binding normally.
`constraint C` declares a constraint and `honor C` names one, so the name
after either keyword is a constraint rather than an ordinary type. This is
the declaration/use duality of spec/constraints.md §4.1 — the subject inside
the following `<...>` is a type and keeps the nominal scope.
A parameterized instance head puts its binders before the constraint name
(spec/constraints.md §4.3: `honor<a: Show> Show<Vector(a)>`), so the name is
no longer adjacent to `honor` and the rule above cannot see it.
The pattern keys on the shape rather than on `honor` itself: an uppercase
name between a binder list's `>` and a tight `<` of its own. Angle brackets
are not type application in Hexagon — `Vector(a)` uses parens — so no
ordinary type reaches this shape, but the pattern is not anchored to the
keyword and would also claim a contrived `a > B<c>` comparison.

//line-bail-guard: Not a rule — the note for the pattern the #162 ruling calls the bail-out guard.
Nothing includes this key; it is documentation kept next to what it describes.
A bracket group in a type context has a closing bracket for its `end`, and
TextMate only ever tries the *top* rule's `end`, so an unterminated group used
to run to end of file and repaint everything after it as type parameters (#162).
The fix has two halves, and every rule below carries whichever half applies:
1. Hanging split. A group may span lines only when its opening bracket is the
last thing on its line, so each group rule is two: a *hanging* variant whose
`begin` gains `(?=[ \t]*$)` and keeps the bracket `end`, and a *bounded*
variant whose `end` gains `|$`. Hanging is listed first so it wins where both
could match. The bracket groups this grammar colours hang their opener in
well-formed source — `record P(`, `derives (`, `let p: {`, `fun map<a, b>(` —
so those keep their colour, while `derives (Eq` half-typed cannot leave its
line. Non-hanging multi-line shapes do exist — `Seq({ pull = () =>` in
`stdlib/Seq.hex` — but they open no group that must survive the line, so the
bounded variant reads them correctly. (Corrected 2026-07-31, #177: this said
*every* well-formed multi-line shape hangs, which that file now disproves.)
2. Bail-out guard. A hanging group can still be left unclosed, so its `end` also
takes
— bail at the next line that begins hard against the left margin, opens a
declaration, or opens a union alternative. The `\|(?!>)` arm is safe because
spec/declarations-preamble.md §2 puts union alternatives after the `=`, as
declaration continuations, so no well-formed bracket group ever contains a
line-leading `|`; the grammar's only other bar rule is the `|>` pipeline
operator. The keyword list is §4.1's `storage.type` and import inventories.
The closing bracket comes first in every hanging `end` alternation: leftmost
alternative wins at equal positions, so a `)` in column zero closes its group
rather than tripping the `^\S` arm.
Everything that can enclose a hanging group takes the guard as well, and for one
reason: an `end` that can only match at `$` cannot fire at position zero, which
is exactly where a bail leaves the enclosing rule on top. So the guard is also on
#type-alias-declaration, on #annotation-type, and on the *bounded* variants —
`let x: Vector(a, (` nests a hanging group inside a bounded one, and without the
guard on the bounded end the bail-out line stays inside `Vector(`'s group to its
own end of line. A bounded end is only ever tried at position zero after an inner
group popped there, so that arm costs nothing anywhere else.
The guard is spelled out in full at each site because TextMate has no way to
share a subpattern; grammar.test.ts pins every copy byte-identical.
What this costs: a group with content on its opening line that then wraps.
`record P derives (Eq,` / `    Show)` still paints `Show`, in the nominal family
rather than the constraint family. Writing it in the hanging form restores it.
A trailing comment counts as content — `record Pair( (* note *)` classifies as
bounded, so its parameters on the next line paint as terms. Same trade, same fix.
Second guard, from #171: every `\(`-based `begin` here also carries `(?!\*)`, so
a `(*` comment opener is never eaten as a bracket. Include order cannot substitute
for it, because #type-declaration-parameters and the `derives` rules start matching
before their `(` and would claim the `(` of `record Pair (* note *)` ahead of
#comments. Exactly two of the seven change any paint — the *bounded*
#type-declaration-parameters rule and the *bounded* `derives` rule. The hanging
variants cannot read a `(*` opener as end of line, #type-expression lists #comments
first, and #type-parameter-bound's nested group is reached only from a context that
now does too. The guard is written out at all seven so every site reads the same;
grammar.test.ts pins those copies too.
Keeping the opener out of a group's `begin` is only half of it. A group's own
`patterns` are the only rules tried inside it, so each of these bodies also
includes #comments — without that, `(*` inside the group falls through to
#punctuation and the `*)` closes the group at its `)`, which loses the colour the
group exists to give and paints the closer as a stray bracket.
One consequence, recorded so it is not read later as a regression: in illegal
source like `record Pair(a *)`, the `*)` is now the unmatched-closer error §3
requires rather than a bracket that closes the group, so the rest of that line
stays type context.

//: Unlike nominal declarations, a type alias has a type expression as its whole
right-hand side, so the header opens a type context.
That context ends at end of line. Running it to the next top-level declaration
instead would be wrong wherever `type` appears indented — Collections Part 2
§5.1 puts an implied type member inside a `constraint` body or `honor` block,
and §5.3's example is indented, so an unbounded context swallows the rest of
the block and paints its member names and parameters as type variables. A
multi-line alias right-hand side is the rarer case and loses only colour.
`$` alone does not deliver that, which is what #162 was: while a group inside
the right-hand side is open, that group is the top rule and this `end` is never
tried, so the bail-out guard is here too. See the //line-bail-guard note.
Data-declaration headers use parentheses, unlike function and constraint
type parameters. Inside this syntactically closed position every
non-uppercase-start name is a type variable (Declarations Preamble §2.1).
Split hanging/bounded per the #162 ruling; see the //line-bail-guard note.

patterns.//: Hanging: `record P(` with the bracket last on its line, so the list continues.
Bounded: content after the bracket, so an unclosed list stops at end of line.

type-declaration-parameter-list.//: #comments first: a group's own patterns are the only ones tried inside it, so without this a `(*` opener reaches #punctuation and the `*)` closes the group.

//: A variance sigil and the parameter it decorates (spec/declarations-preamble.md
§2.1, #205): `+a` covariant, `-a` contravariant. Matched as one rule so the
claim paints as one thing, and ahead of the bare-parameter rule below, which
would otherwise take the name and leave the sigil unstyled.
The grammar does not check that the declaration is `export opaque`, where the
sigil is the only legal spelling. A grammar colours what is written; hexc is
what refuses a sigil on a transparent declaration, and source being repaired
after that error should still read as what the author meant.
Angle brackets are also comparison operators, so entering this context needs
two guards, because a binder list is written tight while a comparison is spaced.
First, `<` must be followed immediately by an identifier character: every binder
and type-argument list is written `<a>`, `honor<a: Show>`, `isEmpty<a>(v)`, so a
spaced `count < limit and total > (x + y)` is excluded before the tail is even
considered. The function-call rule instead excludes parens from its span, which
is not available here — `<a: (Num, Ord)>` needs them (spec/constraints.md §3).
Second, the closing `>` must be followed by `(` (type arguments before a call),
`=` (a constraint or function head), or an uppercase name (an `honor` head's
prefix binder, §4.3: `honor<a: Show> Show<Vector(a)>`).
The obligation side of a binder: `<a: Ord>` and `<a: (Num, Ord)>`. Everything
uppercase after the colon is a constraint (spec/constraints.md §3), which is the
one constraint position with no keyword announcing it. The bound runs to the
binder separator, so the tuple form's own parens are consumed by a nested
context — otherwise the comma inside `(Num, Ord)` would end the bound early.
That nested group is bounded-only, with no hanging variant: #type-parameters
opens only when the closing `>` is on the same line, so no line can end right
after this `(` while the binder list is open. A hanging variant here would be
dead code. Its `|$` is not — `<a: (Num>` half-typed reaches this rule with no
closer on the line, and that is what stops it leaking. The bail-out guard after
the `|$` is uniformity rather than necessity: nothing here can survive to a line
start for it to fire at. See the //line-bail-guard note.
That is a claim about the group, not about this rule. The bound's own `end` is a
lookahead for the binder separator with no line bound, and #type-parameters'
`end` is a bare `>`, so `fun f<a: (Num> = 1` — where the group's `|$` fires but
the swallowed `>` never closes the binder list — still repaints to end of file.
That predates the split and is unchanged by it; it is filed as #174.

constraint-name.//: An uppercase name in a position the grammar has already established is a constraint.
constraint-name.name: entity.name.type.constraint.hexagon

//: A constrained hole, `_ : Show` and `_ : (Eq, Show)` (closure doc
decisions-ml-dialect-annotations-2026-08.md §4.4). Two things need rules of
their own here. The `_` stands before a colon, so the record-type field rule
below would take it for a field name — `_` is its own token and can never be
one (spec/lexer.md §3.2) — and the names after the colon are constraints,
which #constraint-name scopes and the plain type rule does not.
The suffix is bounded: one reference or one balanced parenthesized list. So
the single form needs no context at all, and only the parenthesized form
opens one — bounded-only, its bail-out arms copied from #type-parameter-bound's
nested group, which is the same conjunction in the binder position. See the
//line-bail-guard note.

patterns.//: The single reference, plain or qualified by a module alias (spec/modules.md §3.3). `(?!\.)` keeps a range's `..` out of the qualifier.
`_ :` with the constraint not typed yet: the hole keeps its own scope while the line is half-written, rather than flickering to a field name.
patterns.name: entity.name.type.parameter.hexagon

//: A colon that is not `:=` opens a type annotation. The surrounding
parameter/result/field syntax supplies the closing delimiter. Within this
context casing is sufficient: a non-uppercase-start name can only be a type
variable (Functions §4.2.1), while record-type field names are the one
lowercase role before a nested colon.
`let x: (` and `let p: {` open a hanging group inside this context, so when one
bails the annotation is the top rule at position zero of the bail-out line and
its `$` arm cannot fire there. Hence the guard; see the //line-bail-guard note.
Each bracket group is split hanging/bounded, hanging first, per the #162
ruling — see the //line-bail-guard note.

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §4.1 hard keywords, grouped as that section groups them.
patterns.name: keyword.control.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §4.1 word operators: Hexagon has no `&&`, `||`, or `!`.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.word.hexagon

//: spec/lexer.md §4.1 reserved redirect words (#147). `true`/`false` are still
hard keywords but no longer produce values: Bool is the prelude union
`False | True`, so an occurrence in value position is an error carrying a
one-token fixit. Name position is §10's other row: #declarations is
included ahead of #keywords, so it would claim `let true = 1` first, and
its name alternatives therefore carry an explicit hard-keyword guard (#154)
so this rule reaches the binder position too. `True`/`False` need no rule —
they are ordinary UpperNames and reach entity.name.type through #names,
exactly like `None`.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.reserved-redirect-word.hexagon

//: spec/lexer.md §4.2: these lex as NonUpperName and mean nothing outside their
position, so each rule pins the position. `let when = True` and `{with = 3}`
must keep reading as an ordinary binding and an ordinary field.

patterns.//: `from` is always followed by a module specifier string.
patterns.name: keyword.other.from.hexagon

patterns.//: `x as y` in imports, foreign aliases, and `p as name` patterns. Something being renamed must precede it, or `let r = as b` would read as a keyword.

//: The tuple form `derives (Eq, Show)`, which only ever follows a declaration
header's name or parameter list. Everything it lists is a constraint
(spec/declarations-preamble.md §2.3), so the clause opens a context rather
than scoping the keyword alone.
Split hanging/bounded, hanging first — see the //line-bail-guard note.

patterns.//: The same clause with content after its `(`, bounded to its line.
The single-name form `derives Eq`, the other half of §2.3.

//: spec/lexer.md §4.2 contextual words (#373). `union` left the hard-keyword
table at the Set step, because Collections Part 4 §6.2 mandates `Set.union`
and a reserved word is unspellable in every binder position. It is a keyword
exactly where the parser treats it as one — a declaration head, which is
always followed by the type's name — and an ordinary name everywhere else,
including `Set.union(a, b)`, `s.union(t)`, a bare `union(a, b)`, `let union`,
and a field `{union = 1}`. The declaration-with-a-name shape is already
scoped by the `(record|union|type|exception)[ \t]+(UpperName)` rule above,
which pairs the word with its type name; this rule is what stops the bare
word being claimed anywhere else.
patterns.name: storage.type.hexagon

patterns.//: `export opaque record` / `export opaque union` only.
patterns.name: storage.modifier.hexagon

//: A match/catch arm guard. spec/pattern-matching.md §3 is emphatic that `when`
is arm syntax and never pattern syntax, so it can only follow a complete arm
pattern — never an opening `(` or a `,`, which is where `Event(when, what)`,
`(when) => ...`, `f(when, g)` and `fun schedule(when: Instant)` all put it.
Requiring the arm's `=>` later on the line is necessary but nowhere near
sufficient on its own, because TextMate cannot see bracket depth.

patterns.//: Record update `{p with x = 3}`; `{with = 3}` is a field, `{with}` a pun, and `let ok = with` an ordinary name.

numbers.//: spec/lexer.md §5. Decimal only; `_` needs a digit on both sides; `n` is BigInt.

patterns.//: `0x`/`0o`/`0b` are errors, not literals: Hexagon v1 has decimal literals only.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.numeric-base.hexagon

patterns.//: A trailing `.` with nothing literal after it: write `1.0`. `1.show()` and `1..2` are fine and must not match here.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.numeric-literal.hexagon

patterns.//: Digits joined to identifier characters: `12cats`, `1nmore`, `1efoo`, `1__0`.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.numeric-literal.hexagon

patterns.//: A leading `.`: write `0.5`. The second dot of `1..2` is excluded by the lookbehind.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.numeric-literal.hexagon

//: A non-uppercase-start name applied to arguments. Also catches a constraint
member's bodyless header, which is spelled the same way. The second alternative
admits an angle-bracket type-parameter list only when a call actually follows
it (`isEmpty<a>(values)`), because spec/lexer.md §8.1 makes `<` the very same
token in a comparison — `count <= 0` must keep reading as a comparison.

parameter.//: A binder followed by its type annotation: parameters, record-type fields, and `<a: Ord>` constraint binders. `:=` is assignment, not an annotation.

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §3.2: bare `_` is its own wildcard token; `_name` is an ordinary name.
patterns.name: variable.language.wildcard.hexagon

patterns.//: An uppercase-start name before an accessor `.` is always a qualifier — a module alias or a companion (spec/modules.md §3.3, §5.3). Terms are never uppercase-start, so this cannot be a field access. `..` and `...` are single tokens (§8.1), so `A..B` is a range and its `A` is an ordinary type name.
patterns.name: entity.name.namespace.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §3.1: one scope for every uppercase-start role. Type, union case, constraint, implied type, and exception are deliberately not distinguished before parsing, so this grammar does not invent a distinction either.
patterns.name: entity.name.type.hexagon

operators.//: spec/lexer.md §8.1, ordered so maximal munch (§8.2) falls out of rule order.

patterns.//: spec/effects.md §2.3: the marked type arrows are one token each, and they stand ahead of `->` so maximal munch reaches them. `!->` and `?->` are not tokens and get no rule — a mark never begins one.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.arrow.linked.hexagon

patterns.//: The call marks (spec/effects.md §3.1), written glued on both sides (Lexer §8.1). The left glue is what this rule keys on — a mark follows the callee it marks — so the lookbehind is an identifier character or a closing bracket, which covers `save!(x)`, `stream.next!()`, the parenthesized `(source.next)!()`, and a `|>` stage's trailing `x |> save!`. A floating mark is deliberately left unpainted: it is a parse error (§9's mark-position row), and colouring it as an operator would tell the reader it is one when no such operator exists. This rule must stay *after* the comparison row: at the `!` of `a != b` both start at the same offset, and order is what decides.
patterns.name: keyword.operator.mark.hexagon

invalid.//: spec/lexer.md §8.3 and §10: characters and runs with no token at all. §10's last row requires *any* invalid character to be one diagnostic, so the final rule is a negated class over the whole legal repertoire rather than a list of the forbidden characters someone thought of.

patterns.//: §8.2 special-cases these so the user is pointed at `not`, `and`, `or`. The `!` and `?` arms carry a lookbehind because both now lex as call marks (spec/effects.md §3.1): a mark *glued* to the callee it marks is a real token and #operators paints it, while one standing on its own is what stays wrong — a prefix `!` takes the `not` redirect the scanner used to give, and a floating `?` takes §9's mark-position error. `?` reaches this rule at all only because it left the catch-all's negated class below.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.operator.hexagon

patterns.//: spec/lexer.md §2.2: space and tab are the only horizontal whitespace. There is no invisible second spelling of an ordinary space.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.whitespace.hexagon

patterns.//: Every character outside the identifier repertoire (§3.1) and the closed punctuation inventory (§8.1). Catches `~`, `'` (§3.2: ML-style `a'` names do not exist), `%`, `^`, a lone `&`, `@`, `#`, backtick, backslash, and §11's own rejected `let 😀 = 1`. `!` and `?` are both excluded here because both lex — `!=`, and the two call marks — and the operator rule above already claims whichever of them stands in the wrong place.
patterns.name: invalid.illegal.character.hexagon

tab-indentation.//: spec/lexer.md §2.2 and §10's first row: a tab anywhere from the start of a line through its first non-whitespace character is a hard error. A tab after a token is legal, and a tab inside a string or comment is content — neither reaches this rule.
tab-indentation.name: invalid.illegal.tab-indentation.hexagon
